docs.title: PyEnsembl
docs.text: PyEnsembl lets you find where genes are located, which transcripts they produce, and their sequences in Python. It uses Ensembl annotations or your own files. Once the data is installed, queries run locally.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Use Python 3.11 or later. Run these commands in a terminal:

python -m pip install pyensembl
pyensembl install --release 93 --species human

The second command downloads and indexes human annotation, transcript and protein data. It can take several minutes. These examples use GRCh38 and Ensembl release 93 so you can reproduce the output; for your own analysis, choose the reference that matches your data.

docs.title: Look up a gene
docs.text:
Run this in Python after installation. It retrieves TP53 by its gene ID:

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease

data = EnsemblRelease(93, species="human")
gene = data.gene_by_id("ENSG00000141510")
print(gene.id, gene.name, gene.contig, gene.start, gene.end, gene.strand)

ENSG00000141510 TP53 17 7661779 7687550 -

The result gives the gene ID, name, chromosome, start, end and strand. TP53 is on chromosome 17, on the minus strand. Coordinates are one-based and include both ends; start is the lower coordinate on either strand.

You can also search with data.genes_by_name("TP53"). It returns a list because a name can match several genes. Gene aliases let you search additional names such as p53.

docs.title: Read protein and transcript sequences
docs.text:
A gene can have several transcripts. Continue in the same Python session with one selected transcript:

transcript = data.transcript_by_id("ENST00000269305")
print(transcript.protein_sequence[:30])
print(transcript.sequence[:30])
print(len(transcript.protein_sequence), len(transcript.sequence))
data.close()

MEEPQSDPSVEPPLSQETFSDLWKLLPENN
GTTTTCCCCTCCCATGTGCTCAAGACTGGC
393 2579

The first two lines show the first 30 amino acids of the protein and the first 30 bases of the transcript's cDNA, which begins with the 5′ UTR. The full sequences have 393 amino acids and 2,579 bases. The cDNA is spliced and already oriented 5′ to 3′, including for minus-strand transcripts. Noncoding or incomplete transcripts may have no protein sequence. Both come from the reference annotation, not from your samples.

data.close() releases the open index files. You can instead write with EnsemblRelease(93, species="human") as data: to close them automatically.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Find genes and transcripts by name, ID, position or biotype, and choose among a gene's transcripts.
  • Get protein and transcript sequences: proteins by ID, coding sequences, UTRs, exons and genomic coordinates.
  • Read genomic DNA for introns or flanking regions. Whole-genome DNA is a separate, optional download.
  • Choose another species, assembly or annotation, or install and manage data from Python, check what is installed and free disk space.
  • Find a method in the API reference.

docs.title: Maintain the assembly catalogue
docs.text: pyensembl/assembly_catalog.json is an offline snapshot of assembly identity, separate from cache naming. assembly.py is the shared resolver used by EnsemblRelease and CLI selection. The catalogue ships in both the wheel and source distribution.

docs.title: Sources and update procedure
docs.text:
Numbered records come from the first 4 KiB of each supported species/release GTF, using genome-version, genome-build, and genome-build-accession. Where headers are absent or omit an accession, the capture script reads the small meta.txt.gz in that release's core database dump. It records the source URL and uses assembly.default, assembly.name, and assembly.accession. Each capture includes the compressed GTF prefix's SHA-256.

Dated records use accession-specific entries in the new platform's species.json, filtered to registered/current and historical assemblies. The GRCh37 2013_09 directory is independently verified and retained even if the bulk catalogue omits it. Species-level breed/strain labels are not copied to every assembly. Registered breed accessions identify their own species entries; general dog/mouse constraints may match a known breed/strain.

Run from a development checkout with its dependencies installed:

python scripts/capture_assembly_metadata.py /tmp/ensembl-assembly-captures
python scripts/build_assembly_catalog.py /tmp/ensembl-assembly-captures
./lint.sh
./test.sh

Capture is an explicit online maintenance command. It never uses the user's genome cache, and never downloads full GTFs, DNA, or sequence indexes. Existing captures are reused, so use a new directory for a completely fresh audit. Inspect upstream errors and the generated diff before committing an update. Metadata acquisition must not become an import-time or constructor operation.

The current snapshot audits 1,311 numbered combinations across 43 registered species and contains 52 dated assembly/provider records. Every numbered entry has a build and full assembly name. Sources do not provide a verified accession for these 75 older combinations:

Species Releases with an unknown accession Human 54 Mouse 54–60 Zebrafish 48–60 Worm 48–70 Macaque (macaca_mulatta) 75–85 Guinea pig 75–89 Malaria parasite Ensembl Genomes 40–44

These gaps are represented in metadata_gaps, and the corresponding assembly_accession is None. A missing accession must not be replaced by the accession of a later assembly. Existing datasets remain usable offline. The guinea pig release 89 core metadata URL was also absent; its GTF still provides its assembly name.

docs.title: New API verification
docs.text:
EnsemblRelease.from_ensembl explicitly calls the new service's /genome/{accession}/explain, /genome/{uuid}/details, and /genome/{uuid}/ftplinks. UUID input skips accession discovery. It validates the returned identity and parses the annotation date/provider from the actual geneset path. Website release labels and genome UUIDs are saved separately.

Human and dog responses captured on 2026-10-20 are in tests/data/assembly_metadata/. Tests also use independently captured GTF headers and JSON/pickle objects generated by the published 2.28.3 wheel. Refresh those fixtures deliberately; do not regenerate old-version fixtures with the implementation being tested.

docs.title: Compatibility checks
docs.text:
Test the inferred and explicit forms, ambiguous breed dates, numbered patch transitions, missing metadata, unknown accessions, API errors, and malformed or conflicting API links. The resolver must keep ordinary construction offline.

New serialization stores the resolved metadata and cache-layout choice. Deserialization restores that snapshot even when a newer catalogue disagrees. Old states retain their prior species selection and receive metadata only in memory. The accession inferred for an ordinary call must never cause its deserializer to switch to the explicit-accession cache layout.

reference_name remains the installed display/cache label. An upstream name change cannot rename it. The unused EnsemblAnnotation class was removed in 2.30.0; its historical cache files remain reusable through EnsemblRelease. Keep existing EnsemblRelease signatures and serialized objects supported. All URL generation and DNA preparation belong to EnsemblRelease.

For release validation, reopen actual old-version installed caches with downloads and parsing forbidden and compare their contents, paths, permissions, inodes, and modification/change timestamps. Run the full suite against an isolated copy of the integration data, never by migrating a user's cache.

docs.title: Annotation comparisons
docs.text:
pyensembl/release_comparisons.json records ten scoped comparisons from twenty complete GTF sources captured on 2026-10-23. It ships with wheels and sdists. To reproduce the comparison in an isolated directory:

python scripts/capture_release_comparisons.py --output /tmp/ensembl-gtf-comparisons

This command downloads approximately 1.2 GiB, with a 1 GiB limit per source. It does not touch installed annotation caches. It verifies dated GTF MD5s, records SHA256 and manifest provenance, hashes gene/transcript ID.version sets, and hashes the sorted multiset of complete normalized GTF rows. Headers and input ordering are excluded; repeated attributes and duplicate rows are retained. A missing version is recorded as unknown, never guessed. Set comparisons include unversioned IDs so missing versions cannot be mistaken for entirely unrelated genes. No annotation or sequence cache is shared based on these comparisons.

Review release_comparisons.json in the output directory before copying it into the package. --summaries-only recomputes relationships from existing complete summaries and saved identifier sets without network access. For a fresh upstream audit use a new directory. The tiny independent excerpts in tests/data/release_comparisons/ test parser behavior, not the complete-source biological claims. A separate regression indexes the same real multi-isoform GTF grouped, coordinate-sorted, and with all child features first.

The preferred list is reserved for reviewed future ordering that supersedes a frozen numbered selection. Every entry must name an exact release, accession, provider, coverage, and evidence-based reason. New directory listings alone must never add these preferences. Keep latest opt-in and serialize its resolved concrete selection.

docs.title: Contributing to PyEnsembl
docs.text: PyEnsembl is open source software under the Apache 2.0 license, and we welcome contributions. Contributed code is assumed to use the same license.

docs.title: Filing issues
docs.text: Check the open issues first, then open a new issue for a bug or feature request. Include your PyEnsembl and Python versions. If the problem involves a particular gene, transcript or locus, name it and the release, e.g. "Missing transcript sequence for BRCA1-002 in Ensembl release 74".

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
• Start a new feature with an issue explaining its scope and rationale, and reference the issue in the PR, e.g. "Closes #123".
  • Follow PEP 8; ./lint.sh runs ruff.
  • Accompany new code with unit tests.
  • Support Python 3.9 and later.
  • Bump the version in pyensembl/version.py in every PR, including documentation-only changes.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/openvax/pyensembl.git
cd pyensembl
pip install -e '.[dev]'
./lint.sh
./test.sh

The dev extra installs pytest, pytest-cov, ruff and build. Most tests need Ensembl data installed first; .github/workflows/tests.yml lists the releases CI installs. Tests use exactly those releases, so other genomes in your cache do not change what they check.

Species assembly ranges are checked against Ensembl's archive. After raising MAX_ENSEMBL_RELEASE, recheck every assembly boundary on the live FTP servers:

PYENSEMBL_NETWORK_TESTS=1 ./test.sh tests/test_species_assemblies.py

Timed benchmarks are opt-in because wall-clock limits depend on the machine and its load. Run them on an otherwise idle machine:

PYENSEMBL_BENCHMARKS=1 ./test.sh tests/test_timings.py -s

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Follow the documentation style guide, then build and check the site:

pip install -e '.[dev,docs]'
./docs.sh  # strict build plus link, anchor and API checks
python scripts/check_docs_examples.py  # needs human release 93

Preview with mkdocs serve and review changed pages at desktop and narrow widths.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: Maintainers merge through a PR and publish from a clean main; see releasing.

docs.title: Documentation style
docs.text: Write for someone selecting reference data, running a query and interpreting the result. Follow the mhctools writing guide and its quiet typography. The site uses MkDocs with Material; API pages use mkdocstrings.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
Put installation and the first useful examples directly on the homepage. Readers should reach a result without having to find a separate tutorial. Use one explicitly selected species, assembly and annotation version. Explain IDs, coordinates, strand and sequence interpretation alongside the output. Task guides cover lookups, transcript structure, selection, custom files, aliases, caches and DNA. Reference pages give complete interfaces and metadata; the Genome page opens with a method overview grouped by what each method returns. Contributor and release workflows live in the root CONTRIBUTING.md and RELEASING.md, which the Contributing pages include.

Use descriptive headings and label guides by the task a reader wants to do. Keep desktop sidebar groups expanded by default so readers can see the available tasks; readers can collapse individual groups. Split pages for substantial tasks or reference material, not for each step of a short example. Order common lookups and sequence tasks before reference selection, cache management and custom-data setup. Use the same reference for the main examples; put examples requiring another species or release after the main workflow. Avoid repeating the sidebar in the page body. Comparison tables should have short entries; place long explanations below them or on linked reference pages.

docs.title: Prose and literal syntax
docs.text:
Use ordinary text for biological concepts, units and library names. Link names on first use in a section and in comparison tables. Reserve inline code for literal API names, parameters, fields, commands, paths and values.

Use code Use ordinary text genes_by_name(), EnsemblRelease Ensembl, annotation, genome assembly strand, gene_id, aliases= Chromosome, transcript, exon, base, amino acid "GRCh38", 93, None Human GRCh38, Ensembl release 93 pyensembl install --release 93 Installation, indexing, cache readiness

Keep scientific qualifications next to their claims: assembly and annotation selection, one-based inclusive coordinates, ambiguity, source provenance and the difference between spliced cDNA and genomic DNA. Matching file names or contig names alone do not prove assembly identity.

docs.title: Examples and presentation
docs.text:
Prefer complete examples with imports and real inputs. State required downloads before queries. Pin data and show output when it helps interpretation. Within a guide, examples may continue one Python session when the page says so; the first example then creates data. Label templates and replaceable paths; do not present them as immediately runnable. Keep working examples, source links, page URLs and linked anchors where practical. README compatibility anchors point to the migrated guidance.

Use system fonts, a readable line length and restrained headings. Wide tables and code blocks may scroll within their containers. Use a callout only when a reader needs a distinct instruction to use an example correctly.

docs.title: Build and review
docs.text:
Install the documentation tools and run the checks from the repository root:

python -m pip install -e '.[dev,docs]'
./docs.sh
python scripts/check_docs_examples.py
./lint.sh
./test.sh

The example check runs every Python block that is followed by a text output block on the home page and the gene and transcript guides, and requires human release 93 installed. ./docs.sh builds strictly and validates rendered internal links, anchors, README links and API coverage. CI performs the docs build on PRs and publishes the site from main. Use mkdocs serve to preview the pages; review the first-use and complete reference pages at desktop and narrow widths, including long signatures and tables. Do not use tests that only repeat documentation configuration values.

docs.title: Maintain genetic-code reference metadata
docs.text: pyensembl/genetic_code_catalog.json is a pinned offline snapshot. It maps the 43 registered Ensembl species/strain entries to verified NCBI taxon IDs and contains 42 taxon records including their species ancestors. The wheel and source distribution include it. Runtime construction, deserialization and annotation never contact a taxonomy service.

docs.title: Evidence and scope
docs.text:
Exact species names, with accession matching when necessary, come from the official Ensembl 116 and Ensembl Genomes 63 species TSV files. Taxonomy uses NCBI EUtils XML: GeneticCode/GCId, MitoGeneticCode/MGCId, and plastid Properties/Property[PropName=pgcode]/PropValueInt. Missing or zero values remain unknown. Lineage records establish parent/strain relationships; we do not treat different sibling taxa as equivalent. The platform's generic species listing may describe one representative strain, so it is not used to assign that strain to every reference assembly.

NCBI gc.prt supplies valid code IDs and names. PyEnsembl does not maintain codon translation tables. See NCBI's genetic-code definitions and taxonomy genetic-code documentation.

The snapshot includes source URLs, SHA256 digests of uncompressed captures and UTC retrieval time. Compressed primary inputs are checked in under tests/data/genetic_codes; they allow deterministic reconstruction and review independent of network changes. Refresh only as an intentional metadata update. Existing serialized reference records retain their pinned assignments after an update.

docs.title: Refresh and verify
docs.text:
Run from a development checkout with dependencies installed, using a new capture directory:

python scripts/capture_genetic_code_metadata.py /tmp/ensembl-genetic-codes
python scripts/build_genetic_code_catalog.py /tmp/ensembl-genetic-codes
./lint.sh
./test.sh

Capture is the only networked step. It downloads bounded metadata, not genomic files, and does not use the genome cache. The builder itself is offline. Review species/taxon mappings, changed compartment assignments, source digests and lineage relationships. Replace the checked-in captures with the reviewed inputs so the reconstruction test continues to validate the published snapshot. Additional supported species should use this source mapping and captured NCBI evidence, not handwritten code-selection rules.

docs.title: Publish a release
docs.text:
Every PR includes a version bump in pyensembl/version.py, including documentation changes. The Release version check compares a PR with current main, existing tags, and PyPI. It is required on an up-to-date branch; if another PR merges first, update the version and rerun CI before merging. Once lint, tests and review have passed:

  1. Merge the PR into main.
  2. Check out main, pull the merged commit, and ensure the working tree is clean.
  3. Run ./deploy.sh. It reruns lint and tests, builds the package, checks that main is clean and current and the version is still new, uploads to PyPI, and pushes the version tag.

The release is shipped after the upload succeeds. Documentation changes also publish through the Documentation workflow; check the live site after it runs.

Source archives include the test package and its tracked fixtures. When adding a fixture, add its exact path to MANIFEST.in; avoid recursive fixture globs, which can package generated caches or developer-local data. CI and deploy.sh extract the sdist and run offline tests before upload. To check locally:

python -m build --sdist
python scripts/check_sdist.py dist/pyensembl-*.tar.gz

From a Git checkout this also verifies all tracked test inputs against the archive and rejects extra test files. The extracted archive can run its own ./lint.sh and ./test.sh; the full suite still needs the Ensembl datasets listed in the Tests workflow.

docs.title: Look up gene name aliases
docs.text:
Exact-name lookup uses the symbols in your annotation. To search aliases and previous human symbols too, load the HGNC complete set with one call. PyEnsembl downloads it once and reuses the cached file:

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease, GeneNameAliases

data = EnsemblRelease(93, species="human")  # install this release first
aliases = GeneNameAliases.download_hgnc()
genes = data.genes_by_name("p53", aliases=aliases)
print([gene.name for gene in genes])
data.close()

['TP53']

Names are case-sensitive, including HGNC's lowercase p53 alias. Alias data is human-only and comes from HGNC independently of Ensembl. Only genes present in the annotation are returned, with their original IDs. Ambiguous aliases return all matching genes, including exact-name matches; do not assume the first one is the intended locus. gene_ids_of_gene_name(..., aliases=aliases) returns just the IDs.

docs.title: Reuse or select a snapshot
docs.text:
Cached aliases work offline. They are stored under aliases/homo_sapiens/hgnc in the PyEnsembl cache. Use cache_directory_path= to choose another directory, or overwrite=True to refresh the current complete set explicitly.

For reproducible work, keep the snapshot with your analysis. Current HGNC names can differ from an older Ensembl release. Load a selected local snapshot with GeneNameAliases.from_hgnc("hgnc_complete_set.txt"), or pass an archived HGNC TSV URL as source_url= to download_hgnc(). Plain and gzip TSV files are supported.

docs.title: Other species or custom names
docs.text: Pass your own name-to-gene-ID mapping, for example data.genes_by_name("old_name", aliases={"old_name": ["gene_id"]}).

docs.title: Choose an assembly and annotation
docs.text:
Use EnsemblRelease for both numbered Ensembl releases and dated annotations from the new Ensembl platform. Pin the annotation release for reproducibility. The assembly is normally inferred from the species and selected release:

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease

human = EnsemblRelease(75)                              # GRCh37.p13
current = EnsemblRelease("2026_04", species="human")    # GRCh38.p14
dog = EnsemblRelease("2020_10", species="dog")          # ROS_Cfam_1.0
historical = EnsemblRelease("2013_09", species="human")  # GRCh37.p13

Construction is offline and does not create cache directories. Call download() and then index() to install a dataset; existing installations remain usable in place. Use custom genomes for your own matched GTF and FASTA files.

docs.title: Numbered releases
docs.text:
PyEnsembl supports numbered releases through Ensembl 116 and Ensembl Genomes 63. Common and Latin species names are accepted. The species/release mapping selects the historical assembly, including its actual patch revision where recorded by Ensembl.

pyensembl available
pyensembl install --release 75 --species human
pyensembl install --release 104 --species dog

Human release 75 uses GRCh37.p13; human release 93 uses GRCh38.p12. Dog release 104 uses CanFam3.1, while 105 uses ROS_Cfam_1.0. An explicit assembly assertion must agree with the release:

EnsemblRelease(75, assembly="GRCh37.p13")  # accepted
EnsemblRelease(75, assembly="GRCh38")     # raises ValueError

The existing --reference-name GRCh37 shortcut selects human release 75 when no release is supplied. genome_for_reference_name("GRCh37") prefers an installed release, then a downloaded release, then the newest supported numbered release. Installed dated releases participate, including explicit accession/provider layouts; an installed numbered release keeps precedence. Selection reads existing caches without changing them. Deletion commands require a concrete release and reject latest.

docs.title: Dated releases
docs.text:
A date such as "2026_04" identifies an annotation directory, not a website release. A website label such as "2026-07" is a different identifier and is rejected by the ordinary constructor.

pyensembl install --release 2026_04 --species human
pyensembl install --release 2013_09 --assembly GRCh37

Selection preserves the registered default when it has that date. When the bundled catalogue identifies a unique historical dataset, it can infer that assembly instead: human 2013_09 selects GRCh37.p13. An existing cache directory, old serialized selection, or custom mirror retains its previous selection. Unknown dates retain the existing default selection; absence from the bundled catalogue is not proof that a newly published date does not exist.

To discover dates for the registered default assembly:

from pyensembl import available_dated_releases, available_annotation_dates

available_dated_releases("human")
available_annotation_dates("GCA_000001405.14", "ensembl")

These explicit discovery functions fetch and cache directory listings on first use, then support offline reuse. refresh=True checks again. Ordinary dataset construction does not fetch these listings. A missing remote file produces an UnpublishedDateError with available dates when discovery confirms that the annotation date is absent.

Dates are not a universal chronology: Arabidopsis uses 2010_09, and fly's dated 2022_07 annotation predates its final numbered annotation. Matching assemblies do not make two annotations equivalent. There is no automatic conversion between numbered and dated releases or rolling default. For example, human 2024_11 is a GENCODE subset without non-canonical lncRNA transcripts; numbered release 114 contains the complete annotation.

docs.title: Unified catalogue and opt-in latest
docs.text:
from pyensembl import available_releases

rows = available_releases("human")
chosen = EnsemblRelease("latest", species="human")  # concrete release 116
older = EnsemblRelease("latest", assembly="GRCh37")  # concrete release 75

available_releases combines numbered and dated entries for one assembly. Without an assembly selector, it uses the species' latest numbered assembly; tomato therefore stays on SL4.0. Build names, patched names, accessions, and species constraints follow the ordinary constructor. Each entry includes assembly identity, provider, coverage, subset status, comparison evidence, and whether it is the latest choice. Numbered entries followed by dated entries are a display grouping, not a cross-platform chronological ordering.

The catalogue reads bundled metadata and any cached dated listings offline. refresh=True explicitly fetches listings. Dates discovered after the bundled comparison audit appear as uncompared; they cannot displace a frozen numbered release merely because their date looks recent.

latest is opt-in and conservative: use the newest frozen numbered release for the selected assembly unless a reviewed ordering explicitly supersedes it. Prefer numbered data on verified ties. Supplying provider= or include_alt= restricts selection to the dated platform; within one accession/provider it chooses the newest known date, excluding known subsets. Ambiguous dated scopes require an accession/provider. Existing no-argument and CLI defaults stay the same. Use from_ensembl below for current platform discovery through the API.

The result stores a concrete .release and resolved metadata, including the selection policy. JSON and pickle restore that snapshot without resolving latest again. Keep that serialized object or record its concrete arguments for reproducible analyses.

pyensembl available --species human
pyensembl available --assembly GRCh37 --json
pyensembl available --species dog --refresh
pyensembl install --release latest --species dog

Unfiltered pyensembl available retains the all-species overview. Filtered catalogue output is offline unless --refresh is requested.

docs.title: What the comparisons establish
docs.text:
The October 2026 audit compares complete GTF files, not just their headers or row counts. Human GRCh38 uses the including-alt GTF; other rows use the ordinary GTF selected by EnsemblRelease. Equality excludes headers and row order but includes all data columns, attributes, and duplicate rows.

Species Numbered ↔ dated Verified relationship Human GRCh38 110 ↔ 2023_03, 115 ↔ 2025_12, 116 ↔ 2026_04 Same normalized GTF records Human GRCh38 114 ↔ 2024_11 Dated transcript IDs are a strict subset; 158,710 numbered transcripts absent Human GRCh37 75 ↔ 2013_09 Different; the numbered source also omits ID versions Mouse 116 ↔ 2026_04 Same normalized GTF records Dog 116 ↔ 2020_10 Same gene/transcript ID.version sets; different GTF records Yeast 116 ↔ 2018_10 Same normalized GTF records Fly 116 ↔ 2022_07 Different gene/transcript sets Arabidopsis 63 ↔ 2010_09 Same gene/transcript ID.version sets; different GTF records

These comparisons make no claim about FASTA sequence equality. Primary-only human selections do not inherit including-alt evidence. Even identical GTF records do not alias or merge annotation caches. Source URLs, checksums, counts, set differences, and reproducible capture instructions are described in the assembly catalogue maintenance guide.

docs.title: Dated annotation integrity
docs.text:
New downloads from the canonical dated platform verify each compressed GTF, cDNA, and peptide file against its provider's geneset/md5sum.txt before publishing the file. A receipt records the source MD5, manifest URL/digest, and retrieval time. JSON/pickle pin recorded checksums. Downloading a pinned source with a changed upstream MD5 fails; explicit overwrite=True accepts a new acquisition after validating it against the current manifest.

Existing complete caches retain their original offline path. Normal reuse neither fetches manifests nor adds receipts, changes paths, or rebuilds indexes. Mirrors and numbered downloads keep their existing acquisition behavior.

reports = current.verify_sources()                   # read local files only
reports = current.verify_sources(check_remote=True)  # also read upstream manifests

pyensembl verify --release 2026_04 --json
pyensembl verify --release 2026_04 --check-remote

Verification never repairs or rewrites data. Each source reports verified, changed, unrecorded, invalid-receipt, or an availability failure such as missing or inaccessible. unrecorded means no checksum was captured when the source was acquired; it is not a corruption finding. A present but invalid receipt is reported separately; it is not treated as a legacy file without metadata. Optional upstream results separately distinguish an unchanged manifest entry from a revised one. The command exits with status 1 for a failed source/receipt check or changed upstream checksum, and 0 for verified or unrecorded sources. MD5 detects accidental changes; it is not cryptographic proof of authenticity. These checks cover annotation sources; reference DNA has its separate checksum/index verification.

Known subsets such as human 2024_11, and API annotation labels ending in _subset, produce a warning. annotation_is_subset exposes that status. annotation_label preserves the provider's API label when supplied; it is separate from .release and the existing .annotation_version compatibility field, which both identify the selected PyEnsembl release.

docs.title: Explicit assemblies and dog breeds
docs.text:
Use an assembly argument when the requested date is ambiguous, when selecting a nondefault assembly, or to assert the assembly your analysis requires. All three forms below identify the same GRCh37.p13 assembly:

EnsemblRelease("2013_09", assembly="GRCh37")
EnsemblRelease("2013_09", assembly="GRCh37.p13")
EnsemblRelease("2013_09", assembly="GCA_000001405.14")

A broad name resolves the patch appropriate to the dataset. It does not mean the newest patch in every historical release. Conflicting species, build, patch, and accession arguments raise ValueError before acquisition.

Dog breeds remain distinct assemblies. Basenji and Great Dane both publish an annotation dated 2019_08, so EnsemblRelease("2019_08", species="dog") asks for a more specific selection:

basenji = EnsemblRelease("2019_08", assembly="Basenji_breed-1.1")
great_dane = EnsemblRelease("2019_08", assembly="UMICH_Zoey_3.1")

Species is inferred from known exact selections. Registered breed aliases also work, such as species="dog_basenji". An unregistered accession remains usable, but does not acquire human identity merely because human is the ordinary constructor default.

docs.title: Assembly metadata
docs.text:
These read-only attributes come from one resolved metadata record, regardless of whether the assembly was inferred or supplied explicitly:

Attribute Meaning Human release 75 assembly Build/coordinate-system identifier GRCh37 assembly_name Complete official name, including patch when present GRCh37.p13 assembly_accession Exact versioned GCA/GCF accession GCA_000001405.14 reference_name Existing display/cache compatibility label GRCh37 release Concrete annotation release 75

Names such as CanFam3.1 and ROS_Cfam_1.0 retain their meaningful version suffixes. reference_name is deliberately independent of the official name: for example, the old fly cache label remains BDGP6.54 while the dated platform calls the assembly BDGP6.46.

The bundled catalogue covers every registered numbered species/release and known dated assemblies. Some historical sources do not publish an accession; assembly_accession is None for those entries. Unknown custom accessions can also have unknown names or species. See the catalogue coverage notes. Missing information is never replaced with a guessed identifier or a mandatory network lookup.

JSON and pickle preserve the resolved metadata and cache selection. Reloading an object does not reinterpret it against a changed catalogue. Historical saved objects are enriched in memory without rewriting existing files.

docs.title: Discover through the new Ensembl API
docs.text:
Use this explicitly online entry point for a genome UUID or accession known to the new platform:

data = EnsemblRelease.from_ensembl("GCA_014441545.1")
print(data.assembly_name)    # ROS_Cfam_1.0
print(data.release)          # annotation date, currently 2020_10
print(data.genome_id)        # pinned genome UUID
print(data.website_release)  # separate website release label

An accession lookup selects the entry currently returned by Ensembl; a UUID selects that specific entry. The resulting object records the concrete date, UUID, assembly metadata, and website label for offline serialization. Species and assembly constraints can be supplied and are checked.

Discovery uses the new metadata API's genome details and FTP links. Downloads still use the accession-based bulk GTF/FASTA tree. It does not use the frozen legacy REST service to find new annotations, or require GraphQL for queries. API errors and conflicting metadata are reported rather than silently choosing a different genome.

docs.title: Coverage, DNA, and existing caches
docs.text:
Existing species-based dated calls keep their defaults: human GRCh38 uses genes-including_alt.gtf.gz; other assemblies use genes.gtf.gz. Explicit accession selections default to primary annotation coverage. Use include_alt=True only when that dataset publishes the including-alt file. The cDNA FASTA contains all transcript biotypes. Different providers can publish different file sets; use Genome for nonstandard collections.

Numbered human GRCh38 from release 82, mouse GRCm38 releases 82–102, and zebrafish GRCz11 from release 92 use their complete chr_patch_hapl_scaff GTF. Dated zebrafish has no including-alt counterpart, so its annotation coverage is narrower. Alternative loci can add gene-name matches; prefer stable gene IDs or a contig filter when selecting a particular locus.

Reference DNA is optional: pass genome_fasta=True and optionally genome_fasta_mask="none", "soft", or "hard". Dated datasets publish only toplevel DNA. Read genomic DNA for sequence queries.

Species-based calls retain locations such as GRCh38/ensembl2026_04/. Explicit-accession calls retain the original accession/provider/coverage layout. A named assertion of the default assembly keeps the species layout; an explicit accession uses the accession layout. Supplying cache_directory_path requires a distinct directory per dataset.

Existing data and indexes are not renamed, copied, migrated, or rebuilt by this API change. Shared DNA caching continues to share new verified downloads while preserving existing private copies. No reinstall is needed.

docs.title: Tomato numbered and dated assemblies
docs.text: Tomato illustrates why numbered and dated assembly defaults are separate: EnsemblRelease(63, species="tomato") selects SL4.0, while the registered dated EnsemblRelease("2018_10", species="tomato") retains SL3.0 and its existing cache path. SL4.0 publishes cDNA and peptide FASTAs without a separate ncRNA FASTA. PyEnsembl declares that source difference explicitly; other missing required files remain errors.

docs.title: Removed constructor
docs.text:
EnsemblAnnotation was removed in 2.30.0. Select the same dataset with:

EnsemblRelease(date, assembly_accession=accession, **options)

The equivalent call reuses its existing cache files, including custom labels, directories, and coverage. No reinstall or migration is needed. Imports and serialized objects naming the removed class are no longer supported; recreate the dataset using EnsemblRelease. Existing EnsemblRelease saved objects continue to load.

Ensembl's transition announcement describes the frozen numbered services and the new platform. Both remain accessible through this one constructor.

docs.title: Install and manage data
docs.text: PyEnsembl downloads annotation and sequence files once and indexes them in a local cache. After that, queries need no network access.

docs.title: Install data
docs.text:
Install from the command line:

pyensembl install --release 93 --species human

or from Python, for example in a notebook or pipeline:

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease

data = EnsemblRelease(93, species="human")
data.download()
data.index()

Both skip files that are already downloaded or indexed, so rerunning finishes an interrupted install. install prints one progress line per step on stderr, with progress bars in a terminal; add --verbose (-v) to see every download and database step. In Python, pass show_progress=True to download() and index(). Use --overwrite or overwrite=True to replace existing files.

Choose a reference explains release, species and assembly options. Whole-genome DNA is a separate download.

docs.title: Check what is installed
docs.text:
pyensembl list

Species  Assembly  Release  Annotation   Reference DNA      Location
human    GRCh38    81       indexed      toplevel, indexed  ~/Library/Caches/pyensembl/GRCh38/ensembl81
human    GRCh38    82       not indexed  -                  ~/Library/Caches/pyensembl/GRCh38/ensembl82
custom   GRCm38    mine1    indexed      -                  ~/Library/Caches/pyensembl/GRCm38/mine1

The Annotation column shows whether a release is ready to query:

Annotation Meaning indexed Everything is downloaded and indexed; queries need no network access or setup not indexed Files are downloaded, but the first query would spend minutes indexing them incomplete Some downloads are missing invalid A source is empty or not a regular file inaccessible A source cannot be read

Run pyensembl install for that release to finish. Add --species for non-human genomes; custom genomes need their original install options.

In Python, installed() is True when everything a genome is configured with, reference DNA included, is downloaded and indexed. It only reads the cache. genome_for_reference_name picks the newest installed release of an assembly, else the newest downloaded one, else the newest supported Ensembl release:

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease, genome_for_reference_name
EnsemblRelease(93).installed()
genome_for_reference_name("GRCh38")

# Ensembl releases with any files in the cache, ready or not:
from pyensembl.shell import collect_all_installed_ensembl_releases
collect_all_installed_ensembl_releases()

docs.title: Cache location
docs.text:
PyEnsembl keeps all of its data under one directory, with a subdirectory per genome (<reference>/<annotation><version>, e.g. GRCh38/ensembl81). By default this is the platform cache directory that datacache chooses: ~/.cache/pyensembl on Linux, ~/Library/Caches/pyensembl on macOS, and %LOCALAPPDATA%\pyensembl\pyensembl\Cache on Windows. Releases that PyEnsembl 2.16 or earlier installed on Windows stay in their old per-genome directories and keep working. To use another location, set PYENSEMBL_CACHE_DIR; the data then goes in its pyensembl subdirectory:

export PYENSEMBL_CACHE_DIR=/custom/cache/dir

In Python, set os.environ["PYENSEMBL_CACHE_DIR"] before creating a genome.

New annotation and transcript/protein FASTA downloads have a SHA-256 prefix identifying the complete source URL and decompression mode, followed by the remote filename (for example, <key>-annotation.gtf.gz). Their SQLite and FASTA indexes retain that prefix. URLs with different hosts, paths or query parameters use separate new files, even in the same genome directory. Changing a signed URL also selects a new cache entry. Query parameters and credentials are included in the hash but are not copied into the filename.

Existing installations remain usable in place. Version 2.27.8 restores reuse of basename-only downloads and their original indexes, correcting the 2.27.5 regression. No reinstall, migration, renaming, provenance rewrite or reindexing is required, including for read-only shared caches. Files already downloaded with URL-specific names also remain usable and take precedence when both layouts exist. The shared reference-DNA store keeps its existing behavior.

Legacy entries retain their historical basename lookup and source assumptions, including installations from mirrors. Their original full URL cannot always be recovered from absent or redacted provenance. The new URL-identity guarantee applies to the new layout. If you explicitly need to acquire a different URL despite an existing legacy basename, use download(overwrite=True) or pyensembl install --overwrite: the download uses a URL-specific destination and leaves the legacy files intact. New --custom-mirror downloads belong to that mirror's URLs; use the same mirror to access them through the CLI.

docs.title: Local transcript and protein FASTA indexes
docs.text:
Starting with 2.28.2, new local FASTA indexes identify both the original absolute source path and a SHA-256 of the indexed bytes. Two local files named sequences.fa can safely use the same cache directory. Changed bytes select a fresh index even if the file size and modification time stay the same; older index generations are retained until explicit deletion. New cached copies also identify their original paths and remain usable when the original file disappears. Call download() or index() to refresh a copied input.

Existing basename-only local copies and pickle indexes continue to work in place, including in read-only caches. No migration or reindexing is required. Their original source identity cannot be recovered reliably, so they retain the historical basename assumptions; the new isolation guarantee applies to new entries. Explicitly deleting an index and reindexing adopts the new layout. Refreshing a changed legacy copy writes a new destination and leaves the legacy files intact.

docs.title: Reuse a mirror installation
docs.text:
For a flat directory containing the original Ensembl filenames, install with an explicit mirror:

pyensembl install --release 75 --species human --custom-mirror https://github.com/openvax/ensembl-data/releases/download/GRCh37.75/

In later Python processes, select that same source with with_mirror:

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease

mirror = "https://github.com/openvax/ensembl-data/releases/download/GRCh37.75/"
data = EnsemblRelease(75, species="human").with_mirror(mirror)
assert data.installed()
print(data.gene_by_id("ENSG00000141510").name)

with_mirror returns a Genome whose GTF, transcript and protein URLs point at the mirror. Pass this object explicitly to downstream tools; for example, Variant("1", 53513530, "A", "C", genome=data) in Varcode. To reuse the data through the CLI, repeat --custom-mirror for the same release and species. Requested Ensembl reference DNA is also read from the mirror; explicitly attached local DNA is preserved.

New mirror installations do not populate the source-specific cache used by EnsemblRelease(75) or Varcode's genome=75. If those default constructors are needed, install canonical sources with pyensembl install --release 75 --species human. Existing URL-specific mirror installs from 2.27.5 onward need no redownload or reindexing when opened with the same mirror. The legacy basename-cache compatibility behavior described above still applies; this API does not copy indexes or change existing files' source identity.

docs.title: Free disk space
docs.text:
pyensembl delete-index-files --release 93  # keep downloads, reindex on use
pyensembl delete-all-files --release 93    # all of release 93's files
pyensembl prune --dry-run                  # list unused shared DNA
pyensembl prune

Add --species for non-human releases.

Compatible releases share one copy of Ensembl DNA, so deleting a release keeps DNA that other releases still use, and prune removes DNA that no release references. prune skips DNA that is being downloaded or indexed, never touches local FASTA files, and deletes nothing if any release's DNA metadata is malformed (pyensembl list shows which one).

delete-index-files keeps shared DNA indexes because other releases may use them; rebuild one with index_genome_fasta(overwrite=True). In Python, prune_genome_fastas(dry_run=True) returns (path, bytes) candidates, and pyensembl list --check-genome-fasta verifies each release's DNA index.

docs.title: Inspect files without installing
docs.text:
Inspect a selected genome's source files and indexes, including paths, availability, sizes and any recorded download provenance:

pyensembl inspect --release 93
pyensembl inspect --release 93 --with-genome-fasta --json
# Custom genomes use the same --gtf / --transcript-fasta / --protein-fasta
# and --reference-name / --annotation-name options as install.

In Python, EnsemblRelease(93).inspect_data() returns annotation and optional reference-DNA readiness, installed, and a files dictionary keyed by role (for example gtf, gtf_index, transcript_fasta_1). Values are datacache FileInspection objects with path, status, error, size, mtime, source_url, fetched_at, recorded_sha256 and verified fields. CLI JSON is an array of reports, with errors rendered as strings. Add --check-genome-fasta (Python: check_genome_fasta=True) to validate existing DNA indexes more thoroughly.

Inspection only reads: no network, copying, directory creation, indexing or pickle deserialization. It checks that source files are readable, regular and nonempty and that SQLite indexes are complete; it does not validate biological contents. Recorded provenance is advisory, not a trusted checksum, and files from older versions have none. Downloads are published atomically, so a failed overwrite keeps the previous file; replace an invalid file with pyensembl install --overwrite.

docs.title: Share a cache
docs.text:
Reads take no locks and write nothing, so a fully installed and indexed cache can be read-only for other users. A download or index build locks only the file it writes; registering, deleting and pruning releases briefly lock the whole cache.

New files and lock files follow your umask, so set umask 002 (or default ACLs) before installing into a group-shared cache. Files downloaded before PyEnsembl 2.13.1 were readable only by their owner; share them with chmod -R g+rX "$PYENSEMBL_CACHE_DIR/pyensembl" (or the platform cache directory). dna_cache may be a symlink, e.g. to a larger disk.

docs.title: How reference DNA is stored
docs.text:
Ensembl DNA is stored once per upstream file under pyensembl/dna_cache/:

pyensembl/dna_cache/
  homo_sapiens/ftp.ensembl.org/GRCh38-GCA_000001405.18/
    toplevel/unmasked/fasta/<file key>/
      sequence.fa        uncompressed, even when downloaded as .fa.gz
      sequence.fa.fai
      object.json        full identity of the upstream file
      index.json

For numbered releases, before downloading PyEnsembl reads Ensembl's small README and CHECKSUMS files to see whether another release already has the same file. The versioned assembly accession distinguishes assembly patches, and the 16-character file key (a SHA-256 prefix of the assembly, Ensembl's checksum and compressed size) distinguishes upstream revisions. These are metadata checks: Ensembl's Unix checksums are not cryptographic hashes. If the metadata is incomplete, the assembly directory ends in -unverified and each release keeps its own copy. Local FASTA files and custom mirrors are never shared.

For dated releases, new installs read the official genome/md5sum.txt and compressed size. Matching versioned accession, provider, masking, MD5 and size share one download and index across dates. Downloaded compressed bytes must match the MD5 before the FASTA is published. The date is excluded from a verified file identity, so a new annotation date does not duplicate unchanged DNA. Changed checksums select a separate object; missing or ambiguous metadata keeps each source URL separate. These objects live under dna_cache/ensemblorganisms/ftp.ebi.ac.uk/<accession>/<provider>/toplevel/<mask>/fasta/<file key>/.

Existing dated DNA installations remain usable in place. Their private files, indexes and manifests are neither migrated nor rewritten. Repeated download_genome_fasta() and index_genome_fasta() calls reuse them, including offline and read-only caches. New sharing therefore prevents future duplicates; it does not automatically reclaim existing copies. Numbered and dated DNA are not assumed interchangeable solely because their accessions match: their file formats and upstream checksum schemes differ.

Downloads retry transient HTTP failures and stalls of five minutes, and are checked against the upstream size. An interrupted DNA download resumes on the next install on POSIX systems, using only bytes the server confirms come from the same file; on Windows it starts over.

docs.title: Load custom genomes
docs.text: Use Genome with local paths or remote URLs for matched GTF annotations and FASTA sequences. GTF conventions vary between providers; custom-data support depends on the supplied fields. Matching contig names alone do not prove that the files use the same assembly.

docs.title: Index local annotations
docs.text:
This template requires your own GTF and FASTA files. Replace the paths before running it; transcript and peptide record IDs must match the GTF identifiers. Omit sequence sources when you only need annotation lookups.

from pyensembl import Genome

with Genome(
    reference_name="GRCh38",
    annotation_name="my_genome_features",
    annotation_version="1",
    gtf_path_or_url="/data/my_genome_features.gtf",
    transcript_fasta_paths_or_urls=["/data/transcripts.fa"],
    protein_fasta_paths_or_urls=["/data/proteins.fa"],
    cache_directory_path="/data/pyensembl-indexes/my_genome_features-1",
) as data:
    data.index()
    gene_names = data.gene_names_at_locus(contig=6, position=29945884)

Local files are used in place by default, with indexes in the cache. Set copy_local_files_to_cache=True for an independent cached import; decompress_on_download=True also applies to copied sources. Remote sources require data.download() before data.index().

docs.title: Match files and identifiers
docs.text:
Keep annotation source, assembly, version and file provenance with your analysis. A GTF should identify genes and transcripts using gene_id and transcript_id; sequence lookup uses matching FASTA record IDs. Gene-only GTF files can support gene queries without transcript identifiers.

Ensembl IDs match with or without a version suffix, whether the files store versions in separate *_version attributes (Ensembl) or in the IDs themselves (GENCODE). A supplied version must match the stored one. When FASTA headers carry no version, or several versions of one ID, sequence lookups use the version the GTF records; an ID that still matches several versions raises an error.

GFF3 requires conversion to GTF before indexing. Unsupported or missing GTF attributes can limit which queries work. Data inspection checks files and index readiness, not biological validity or assembly identity.

To read genomic DNA, add genome_fasta_path_or_url="/data/reference.fa" using the same assembly. See local reference DNA for compression, read-only source files and contig validation. For a standard new-platform geneset, use Ensembl's dated annotations.

docs.title: Find genes and transcripts
docs.text: These examples use the human GRCh38 / Ensembl release 93 data installed on the home page. They run in one Python session.

docs.title: Find a gene by name or ID
docs.text:
A name lookup returns a list of every matching gene:

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease

data = EnsemblRelease(93, species="human")
for gene in data.genes_by_name("TP53"):
    print(gene.id, gene.name, gene.contig, gene.biotype)

ENSG00000141510 TP53 17 protein_coding

A name can match several loci, such as copies on patch or haplotype contigs. When you know the gene ID, data.gene_by_id("ENSG00000141510") selects it directly. Alias lookup adds names from a separate source, such as HGNC.

docs.title: Versioned IDs
docs.text:
Ensembl IDs can carry a version, which changes when a feature's structure or sequence changes. Every method that takes a gene, transcript, exon or protein ID accepts it with or without one:

gene = data.gene_by_id("ENSG00000141510.16")
print(gene.id, gene.versioned_id)

ENSG00000141510 ENSG00000141510.16

An ID without a version matches whatever version this release has. An ID with a version must match it: data.gene_by_id("ENSG00000141510.15") raises ValueError: ENSG00000141510.15 is not in this annotation, which has ENSG00000141510.16, so an ID copied from another release can't silently match a changed feature. Releases before Ensembl 77 record no versions, so they accept only IDs without one.

docs.title: Find genes at a position
docs.text:
Give a position, or add end to search an interval:

print(data.gene_names_at_locus(contig="17", position=7668402))
for gene in data.genes_at_locus(contig="17", position=7660000, end=7690000):
    print(gene.name, gene.strand, gene.start, gene.end)

['TP53']
WRAP53 + 7686071 7703502
TP53 - 7661779 7687550
AC087388.1 - 7685260 7686371

Coordinates are one-based and inclusive, and must use the selected assembly. Overlapping genes on both strands are returned; pass strand="+" or "-" to restrict the search. transcripts_at_locus and exons_at_locus work the same way, and nearest_gene finds the closest gene when none overlaps.

docs.title: Filter by contig or biotype
docs.text:
Whole-genome lists accept optional contig, strand and biotype filters:

coding_genes = data.genes(contig="17", biotype="protein_coding")
print(len(coding_genes))

1183

Biotype names come from the annotation and can differ between releases; list them with {gene.biotype for gene in data.genes()}. gene_ids, gene_names and transcript_ids return identifiers without building objects, and data.contigs() lists the chromosome and contig names.

docs.title: Choose among a gene's transcripts
docs.text:
A gene usually has several transcripts. List order does not identify a preferred isoform, so choose by ID or by attributes that suit your analysis:

gene = data.gene_by_id("ENSG00000141510")
coding = [t for t in gene.transcripts
          if t.biotype == "protein_coding" and t.complete]
print(len(gene.transcripts), len(coding))
coding.sort(key=lambda t: len(t.protein_sequence), reverse=True)
for t in coding[:3]:
    print(t.id, t.name, t.support_level, len(t.protein_sequence))

28 19
ENST00000269305 TP53-201 1 393
ENST00000445888 TP53-205 1 393
ENST00000615910 TP53-221 5 382

TP53 has 28 transcripts; 19 are protein coding with annotated start and stop codons. support_level is Ensembl's transcript support level, from 1 (best supported by mRNA evidence) to 5, or None when the annotation omits it. Two transcripts can encode the same protein from different UTRs.

docs.title: Sequences and exons
docs.text: Get protein and transcript sequences continues with a transcript's protein, coding sequence, UTRs, exons and codon positions. The method overview lists every lookup. Call data.close() when you are finished; a with EnsemblRelease(93, species="human") as data: block closes it automatically.

docs.title: Fly annotation
docs.text:
This separate example selects fly release 100. Install it before running the Python fragment:

pyensembl install --release 100 --species drosophila_melanogaster

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease

data = EnsemblRelease(100, species="drosophila_melanogaster")
gene = data.gene_by_id("FBgn0011747")
transcripts = gene.transcripts

docs.title: Human release 77: HLA-A
docs.text:
This example uses human release 77. Install its data before querying HLA-A:

pyensembl install --release 77 --species human

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease

data = EnsemblRelease(77, species="human")
print(data.gene_names_at_locus(contig=6, position=29945884))

The result is ["HLA-A"]. Release 77 also uses GRCh38, but its annotation differs from release 93, so pin the release you analyze.

docs.title: Find a reference or transcript's genetic code
docs.text: PyEnsembl exposes NCBI translation-table IDs and their provenance. It does not translate sequences. Use a transcript's assignment when available: a declaration in its annotation takes precedence over the reference default.

docs.title: Reference defaults without downloads
docs.text:
from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease

yeast = EnsemblRelease(116, species="yeast")
assert yeast.taxon_id == 559292           # the S288C reference strain
assert yeast.species_taxon_id == 4932     # Saccharomyces cerevisiae
assert yeast.genetic_code("MT").table_id == 3
assert yeast.genetic_code("unplaced_42").table_id == 1
assert yeast.genetic_code().table_id == 1
assert yeast.genetic_code(compartment="nuclear").table_id == 1

plant = EnsemblRelease(63, species="tomato")
assert plant.plastid_translation_table == 11

nuclear_translation_table, mitochondrial_translation_table and plastid_translation_table return an integer or None. The assignments come from a bundled, verified taxonomy snapshot, with independent values for each compartment. Mitochondrial assignments include human/mouse 2, budding yeast 3 and fly/nematode 5; Candida albicans has nuclear table 12. A mitochondrial contig name alone does not select a table. The reference's taxon or an explicit assignment is also needed.

genetic_code() returns an immutable GeneticCodeAssignment with table_id, compartment, source, taxon_id, source_url, and reason. Unknown assignments have table_id=None and an explanation. An omitted contig or an unrecognized name, including an unplaced scaffold, uses the species' nuclear table. This is the species' main code, not necessarily table 1: Candida albicans defaults to table 12. Unknown taxa still need an explicit assignment; they do not silently receive table 1.

docs.title: Transcript source declarations
docs.text:
After the annotation has been installed, read:

transcript = yeast.transcript_by_id(yeast.transcript_ids()[0])
source_only = transcript.source_translation_table
assignment = transcript.genetic_code
effective_id = transcript.translation_table

source_translation_table reads transl_table or translation_table on the transcript and its CDS rows. It returns None when no declaration is present. Repeated agreeing values are accepted; different values or invalid NCBI IDs raise ValueError. A valid source declaration wins over a different taxonomy default or explicit reference default, including on an unplaced scaffold. assignment.source is annotation, reference, taxonomy, or unresolved. For an annotation declaration, source_url identifies the configured GTF path or URL. compartment describes the selected compartment, including the nuclear default; it is not proof of the contig's physical localization.

New annotation indexes retain these optional attributes. Old indexes remain usable unchanged: the first lookup scans the installed GTF for the sparse declarations and keeps them only in memory. There is no download, migration, sidecar, or reindex. If a configured GTF is missing, transcript lookup raises instead of treating that absence as evidence that no source override exists. Reference-only genome.genetic_code() does not need a GTF.

docs.title: Custom references and contigs
docs.text:
One optional reference_metadata argument configures the reference:

from pyensembl import Genome

genome = Genome(
    "study-reference", "study-annotation",
    reference_metadata={
        "taxon_id": 7227,
        "contig_compartments": {"scaffold_42": "mitochondrial"},
        "source_url": "https://example.org/study-reference",
    },
)
assert genome.genetic_code("scaffold_42").table_id == 5
assert genome.genetic_code("unplaced_1").table_id == 1

An optional translation_tables mapping can explicitly set nuclear, mitochondrial, or plastid to a valid integer table ID. None explicitly leaves that compartment unresolved. Unspecified compartments retain their validated taxonomy defaults. Table IDs are metadata: a translation engine may reject codes whose stop/sense behavior needs additional context.

Explicit contig_compartments take precedence. Matching is exact first, then case-insensitive; conflicting case aliases raise. Fallback names are:

Compartment Case-insensitive aliases Mitochondrial MT, M, chrMT, chrM, mito, mtDNA, mitochondrion, mitochondrial, mitochondrion_genome, mitochondrial_genome Plastid Pt, CP, chrC, chrPt, chloroplast, plastid, apicoplast Nuclear Positive chromosome numbers, X, Y, W, Z, Roman numerals I–XVI, and chromosome arms 1L–4R; optionally prefixed by chr

Other names default to nuclear. These names are conventions, not assembly evidence; supply reference metadata for nonstandard organelle names. You can also call genome.genetic_code(compartment="plastid") without a contig. When both are given, an inconsistent known compartment raises rather than ignoring the constraint. An arbitrary scaffold name does not conflict with an explicitly requested compartment. An identified organelle whose table is missing remains unresolved rather than using the nuclear default.

docs.title: Taxonomy and saved objects
docs.text:
Registered species infer taxon identity offline. A custom Genome can infer it from an exact registered reference_name; arbitrary labels and filename fragments are not matched. An EnsemblRelease uses its selected species or source API record, independent of its display label. from_ensembl() retains the API's taxon and species-ancestor IDs and validates known conflicts. Strain/parent differences are accepted only with captured lineage evidence. Unknown positive taxon IDs remain unresolved; they do not trigger requests.

genome.reference_metadata returns a copy of the pinned record, including source URLs, retrieval time and taxonomy digest. JSON, pickle and with_mirror() preserve it. Loading a saved record does not refresh its codes from a newer catalogue. Old saved objects infer metadata in memory. Metadata overrides distinguish in-memory objects, while annotation source URLs, reference labels and disk cache paths stay unchanged. CLI install hints install the same files; custom metadata belongs to the Python object and its serialized record, not the on-disk installation.

docs.title: Read genomic DNA
docs.text: Reference DNA lets you read any genomic interval, including introns, intergenic regions and flanking sequence. It is optional: a normal installation does not download a whole genome. Human DNA is about 1 GB to download and takes several GB of disk once decompressed.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
# Annotation and DNA, or just the DNA:
pyensembl install --release 93 --species human --with-genome-fasta
pyensembl install --release 93 --species human --only-genome-fasta

from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease

data = EnsemblRelease(93, species="human", genome_fasta=True)
data.download_genome_fasta()  # does nothing if the DNA is already installed
with data:
    bases = data.sequence("7", 117_480_000, 117_480_100)
    tp53 = data.gene_by_id("ENSG00000141510")  # TP53, on the minus strand
    tp53_dna = data.sequence(
        tp53.contig, tp53.start, tp53.end, strand=tp53.strand
    )

genome_fasta=True only chooses the DNA. Nothing is downloaded until you call download_genome_fasta() or download(), or run pyensembl install. Python objects use reference DNA only when constructed with genome_fasta: a plain EnsemblRelease(93) does not pick up DNA installed by the CLI, and its error message names the call that does.

docs.title: Reading sequences
docs.text:
sequence(contig, start, end, mask="upper", *, strand="+"):

  • Coordinates are one-based and inclusive, like the rest of PyEnsembl, with 1 <= start <= end <= contig length.
  • Bases are read from the plus strand; strand="-" returns the reverse complement, so a gene or transcript reads 5' to 3'.
  • Contigs can be named as in the FASTA or as PyEnsembl reports them (gene.contig). If the names differ only by a chr prefix, the error suggests the right one.
  • Results are uppercase; mask="raw" keeps soft-masked repeats in lowercase.
  • Absent contigs and invalid ranges raise ValueError. Missing DNA raises MissingGenomeFastaError, a ValueError whose message explains how to install or enable it. Reads never download anything.

Related attributes and methods:

  • fasta is a pyfaidx reader with zero-based, half-open slices (fasta[contig][start - 1:end].seq), as used by Varcode. It needs the FASTA's own contig names, and is None when DNA is not configured or not installed.
  • genome_fasta_path is the uncompressed FASTA on disk, or None.
  • download() and index() include DNA when it is configured. index_genome_fasta() builds the DNA index before the first query needs it.
  • close() closes the reader. Readers already handed out stay usable after clear_cache().
  • Attached DNA does not affect equality: genes and transcripts from the same release compare equal with or without it.

docs.title: Choosing DNA
docs.text:
Python (EnsemblRelease) CLI (pyensembl install) Ensembl's DNA genome_fasta=True --with-genome-fasta or --only-genome-fasta A local FASTA genome_fasta="/data/ref.fa.gz" --genome-fasta-path /data/ref.fa.gz Coverage genome_fasta_type="primary_assembly" --genome-fasta-type primary_assembly Masking genome_fasta_mask="soft" --masked soft

The default is unmasked toplevel DNA, which covers the patch and haplotype contigs in Ensembl annotations. primary_assembly has the chromosomes and unplaced/unlocalized sequences but no patches or haplotypes, and some older releases and species don't provide it. Masking is none, soft (repeats in lowercase), or hard (repeats replaced with N). See Ensembl's DNA file definitions.

docs.title: Local FASTA files
docs.text:
data = EnsemblRelease(
    93, species="human", genome_fasta="/data/my_reference.fa.gz"
)

# Custom annotations can attach DNA too, from a path or URL:
from pyensembl import Genome
custom = Genome("custom", "my_annotations",
                genome_fasta_path_or_url="/data/reference.fa")

Plain FASTA files are read in place; gzip and BGZF files are decompressed into PyEnsembl's cache on first use. Indexes always live in the cache, so read-only source directories work and your own files and indexes are never modified. index() warns about annotation contigs that are missing from a local FASTA, but matching contig names don't prove that the assembly matches.

docs.title: Disk space and shared files
docs.text: Compatible releases share one copy of Ensembl DNA. To delete DNA, prune unused copies or share a cache with other users, see free disk space and how reference DNA is stored.

docs.title: Get protein and transcript sequences
docs.text: These examples go further than the home page with the TP53 transcript TP53-201. They use the human GRCh38 / Ensembl release 93 data installed on the home page and run in one Python session.

docs.title: Protein sequence
docs.text:
from pyensembl import EnsemblRelease

data = EnsemblRelease(93, species="human")
transcript = data.transcript_by_id("ENST00000269305")
protein = transcript.protein_sequence
print(transcript.versioned_id, transcript.protein.versioned_id, len(protein))

ENST00000269305.8 ENSP00000269305.4 393

protein_sequence is the annotated translation from Ensembl's peptide file. It normally has no stop symbol, but a few peptides, mostly from polymorphic pseudogenes, contain * stop symbols. versioned_id adds this release's version to a stable ID; transcript.protein_id is the stable protein ID without it.

When you start from a protein ID, look up its sequence, transcript or gene directly:

print(data.protein_sequence(transcript.protein_id) == protein)
print(data.transcript_by_protein_id("ENSP00000269305").name)
print(data.gene_by_protein_id("ENSP00000269305").name)

True
TP53-201
TP53

Each lookup also accepts a versioned ID such as ENSP00000269305.4. A version that differs from this release's, such as ENSP00000269305.3, raises ValueError instead of returning this release's protein.

Noncoding transcripts have no protein, so their protein, protein_id and protein_sequence are None:

noncoding = data.transcript_by_id("ENST00000505014")
print(noncoding.name, noncoding.biotype, noncoding.protein_sequence)

TP53-210 retained_intron None

docs.title: Coding sequence
docs.text:
cds = transcript.coding_sequence
print(len(cds), cds[:9], cds[-3:])
print(transcript.complete)

1182 ATGGAGGAG TGA
True

The coding sequence runs from the first base of the start codon through the stop codon, so its 1,182 bases are 393 codons plus the stop. complete is True when the transcript has annotated three-base start and stop codons and a coding length divisible by three.

docs.title: Transcript sequence and UTRs
docs.text:
transcript.sequence is the full spliced cDNA, oriented 5′ to 3′. For a transcript with annotated start and stop codons, it is the 5′ UTR, the coding sequence and the 3′ UTR joined together:

utr5 = transcript.five_prime_utr_sequence
utr3 = transcript.three_prime_utr_sequence
print(len(transcript.sequence), len(utr5), len(cds), len(utr3))
print(transcript.sequence == utr5 + cds + utr3)

2579 190 1182 1207
True

To include introns or flanking sequence, read genomic DNA from the same assembly.

docs.title: Incomplete transcripts
docs.text:
A protein_coding biotype does not guarantee a complete coding sequence. Some transcripts are fragments without an annotated start or stop codon:

fragment = data.transcript_by_id("ENST00000576024")
print(fragment.name, fragment.biotype, fragment.complete)
print(fragment.contains_start_codon, fragment.coding_sequence)
print(fragment.protein_sequence[:10])

TP53-216 protein_coding False
False None
XSPQPKKKPL

Without an annotated start codon, coding_sequence and five_prime_utr_sequence are None. The peptide file can still hold a partial translation, so check complete before analyzing codons or reading frames.

docs.title: Exons
docs.text:
print(transcript.contig, transcript.start, transcript.end, transcript.strand)
for exon in transcript.exons[:2]:
    print(exon.id, exon.start, exon.end)
print(len(transcript.exons))

17 7668402 7687538 -
ENSE00001146308 7687377 7687538
ENSE00002667911 7676521 7676622
11

The transcript's span includes its introns. transcript.exons is in transcription order, so on the minus strand the first exon has the highest coordinates. Every start is still the lower coordinate, and coordinates are one-based and inclusive.

docs.title: Codon positions and coding intervals
docs.text:
print(transcript.start_codon_positions)
print(transcript.stop_codon_positions)
print(transcript.coding_sequence_position_ranges[:2])

[7676592, 7676593, 7676594]
[7669609, 7669610, 7669611]
[(7669609, 7669690), (7670609, 7670715)]

These are genomic positions in ascending order. On the minus strand, translation starts at the highest position of the start codon, 7676594. coding_sequence_position_ranges lists the coding part of each exon, including the stop codon, which Ensembl annotates separately from the CDS.

docs.title: Map a genomic position to the transcript
docs.text:
spliced_offset converts a genomic position inside an exon to a zero-based index into transcript.sequence:

offset = transcript.spliced_offset(7676594)
print(offset, transcript.sequence[offset:offset + 3])
data.close()

190 ATG

The first base of the start codon is at offset 190, immediately after the 5′ UTR. Positions in introns or outside the transcript raise ValueError. The Transcript reference lists every attribute.

docs.title: Command-line reference
docs.text: Run pyensembl ACTION [options]. Installation, assembly selection, data inspection and reference DNA explain the main workflows. Dated releases of the new platform use --release YYYY_MM, e.g. --release 2026_04; other new-platform datasets use the Python constructor described in the platform guide.

docs.title: Commands and options
docs.text:
This is the complete help output for the documented package version. Run pyensembl --help for the version installed in your environment.

usage: pyensembl ACTION [options]

Install and manage the genome data PyEnsembl uses.

positional arguments:
  ACTION                one of the actions listed below

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --version             show program's version number and exit
  -v, --verbose         Show detailed progress, including download and
                        database steps
  --json                With inspect, available, or verify, print JSON
  --overwrite           Force download and indexing even if files already
                        exist locally
  --reference-name REFERENCE_NAME
                        Reference assembly, e.g. GRCh37 (case-insensitive for
                        Ensembl). Selects its newest supported release unless
                        --release is given; with custom source files, names
                        the custom reference.
  --refresh             With available, refresh dated listings from Ensembl
  --check-remote        With verify, compare recorded MD5s with current
                        upstream manifests

Ensembl release options:
  --release RELEASE [RELEASE ...]
                        Ensembl release version(s): numbered, YYYY_MM, or opt-
                        in latest on the new Ensembl platform; required for
                        deletion (install default=newest supported release for
                        --reference-name, otherwise for each species)
  --species SPECIES [SPECIES ...]
                        Which species to download Ensembl data for
                        (default=inferred from --reference-name, otherwise
                        human)
  --assembly ASSEMBLY   Optional build, full assembly name, or versioned
                        GCA/GCF accession
  --assembly-accession ASSEMBLY_ACCESSION
                        Explicit accession (uses the compatible accession
                        cache layout)
  --provider PROVIDER   Annotation provider for a dated release
  --server SERVER       Mirror root preserving Ensembl's directory structure
                        (advanced)
  --include-alt, --no-include-alt
                        Select dated annotation coverage explicitly
  --cache-reference-name CACHE_REFERENCE_NAME
                        Preserve a custom reference label when reopening an
                        accession dataset
  --cache-directory CACHE_DIRECTORY
                        Explicit existing cache directory for one selected
                        dataset
  --custom-mirror CUSTOM_MIRROR
                        Flat mirror URL/directory; repeat it to reuse mirror
                        data. In Python use
                        EnsemblRelease(...).with_mirror(URL). New mirror
                        caches are separate from default EnsemblRelease
                        caches.

Custom genome options:
  --annotation-name ANNOTATION_NAME
                        Name of annotation source (e.g. refseq)
  --annotation-version ANNOTATION_VERSION
                        Version of annotation database
  --gtf GTF             URL or local path to a GTF file containing
                        annotations.
  --transcript-fasta TRANSCRIPT_FASTA
                        URL or local path to a FASTA files containing the
                        transcript data. This option can be specified multiple
                        times for multiple FASTA files.
  --protein-fasta PROTEIN_FASTA
                        URL or local path to a FASTA file containing protein
                        data.
  --shared-prefix SHARED_PREFIX
                        Add this prefix to URLs or paths specified by --gtf,
                        --transcript-fasta, --protein-fasta

Optional reference DNA:
  --with-genome-fasta   Also download and index reference DNA (several GB for
                        human)
  --only-genome-fasta   Download/index only reference DNA, without annotation
                        or transcript data
  --genome-fasta-path GENOME_FASTA_PATH
                        Attach a local reference FASTA; custom Genome sources
                        also accept a URL
  --genome-fasta-type {toplevel,primary_assembly}
                        Toplevel includes patch/haplotype contigs (default)
  --masked {none,soft,hard}
                        Masking of downloaded reference DNA (default: none)
  --check-genome-fasta  With list or inspect, check DNA indexes without
                        downloading or rebuilding
  --dry-run             With prune, report candidates without deleting files

actions:
  install             download and index genome data (skips what is already done)
  list                show installed genomes, whether they are indexed, and their DNA
  inspect             inspect selected source files, indexes, and download provenance offline
  verify              verify recorded dated-annotation checksums without repair
  available           show supported species, assemblies, and Ensembl releases
  delete-index-files  delete indexes, keeping downloaded files (needs --release)
  delete-all-files    delete all of a genome's local data (needs --release)
  prune               delete shared reference DNA that no installed release uses

examples:
  pyensembl install --release 75 77                     human releases 75 and 77
  pyensembl install --release 110 --species mouse       a mouse release
  pyensembl install --release 2026_04                   a dated release (new Ensembl platform)
  pyensembl install --reference-name GRCh37             newest release for GRCh37
  pyensembl install --release 110 --with-genome-fasta   also install reference DNA
  pyensembl install --reference-name GRCh38 --annotation-name my_genes \

docs.title: Errors and exit status
docs.text:
Argument mistakes, such as an unknown species/release, conflicting selectors, or an explicitly empty source path, print a concise argparse error and exit 2. An empty --gtf, FASTA path, --custom-mirror, or --server never falls back to downloading the default Ensembl dataset. Omit an unused option instead; spaces in legitimate file paths are preserved.

Missing annotation files or reference DNA print pyensembl: error: ... and exit 1. Malformed GTF data, corrupt databases, checksum failures, and unexpected internal errors retain their tracebacks for diagnosis. A concrete deletion request with nothing installed remains a successful no-op.

False copy_local_files_to_cache bool

Combined reference DNA FASTA. Supports plain or gzip input; indexes and decompressed copies are stored in the cache.

Species(latin_name, synonyms=[], reference_assemblies={}, division='vertebrates', ensembl_genomes=False, ensembl_names=None, dated_releases=None, dated_reference_name=None, assemblies_without_ncrna=())

Container for combined information about a species name, its synonyn names and which reference to use for this species in each Ensembl release.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default latin_name str required synonyms list of strings [] reference_assemblies dict

Mapping of names of reference genomes onto inclusive ranges of Ensembl releases Example: {"GRCh37": (54, 75)}

{} division str

Ensembl division this species belongs to. One of "vertebrates", "plants", "fungi", "metazoa", "protists", "bacteria". Defaults to "vertebrates".

'vertebrates' ensembl_genomes bool

If True, the species' annotation and FASTA files live on the Ensembl Genomes server (ftp.ensemblgenomes.ebi.ac.uk) under the /{division}/... subtree, with their own release numbering (1..MAX_ENSEMBL_GENOMES_RELEASE). If False (default) the species is served from the main Ensembl FTP at ftp.ensembl.org.

False ensembl_names dict

Names Ensembl publishes the species under from a given release on, when it renamed it, e.g. {100: "canis_lupus_familiaris"}.

None dated_releases tuple of (str, str)

Assembly accession and provider under which the new Ensembl platform publishes dated releases (e.g. "2026_04") of the registered default assembly, e.g. ("GCA_000001405.29", "ensembl").

None dated_reference_name str

Stable label of that dated assembly when it differs from the latest numbered assembly. Existing dated cache paths retain it.

None assemblies_without_ncrna iterable of str

Numbered assemblies with no separately published ncRNA FASTA. Their transcript sources contain only cDNA. Other missing files remain installation errors.
